column1: State the Axiom of Extensionality formally.
column2: $A = B \iff \forall x \, (x \in A \iff x \in B)$ — two sets are equal iff they contain exactly the same elements.

column1: What is Russell's Paradox and what does it prove?
column2: Let $R = \{x : x \notin x\}$. Then $R \in R \iff R \notin R$, a contradiction. It proves that unrestricted Comprehension (forming $\{x : P(x)\}$ for any property $P$) is logically inconsistent, necessitating axiomatic restrictions on set formation.

column1: Why must the universal set $\mathcal{U}$ be fixed before defining a complement $A^c$?
column2: Because $A^c$ means 'all elements not in $A$,' which is undefined without specifying the domain of discourse. Without a fixed $\mathcal{U}$, complement is incoherent and risks paradox, just as unrestricted comprehension does.

column1: How do union and intersection correspond to logical connectives?
column2: $A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \lor x \in B\}$ corresponds to logical OR; $A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \land x \in B\}$ corresponds to logical AND. Set operations are a formal isomorphism of Boolean logic on membership predicates.

column1: Define a binary relation $R$ on sets $A$ and $B$, and what does $a \mathrel{R} b$ mean?
column2: $R$ is a subset $R \subseteq A \times B$. Writing $a \mathrel{R} b$ means precisely $(a,b) \in R$ — nothing more, nothing less.

column1: Which three properties define an equivalence relation, and what structure do they produce?
column2: Reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. Together they partition a set into non-overlapping equivalence classes.

column1: What distinguishes a partial order from an equivalence relation in terms of defining properties?
column2: A partial order replaces symmetry with antisymmetry, while keeping reflexivity and transitivity — producing a hierarchy of comparability rather than a partition into classes.

column1: Give the set-theoretic definition of a function $f: A \to B$.
column2: $f$ is a relation $f \subseteq A \times B$ such that for every $a \in A$, there exists exactly one $b \in B$ with $(a,b) \in f$. A function is a relation constrained by unique output per input.

column1: What is the defining difference between a partial order, total order, and well-order?
column2: Partial order: elements may be incomparable. Total order: every pair is comparable (trichotomy holds). Well-order: a total order where every non-empty subset has a least element.

column1: What is the only coherent definition of 'same cardinality' between two sets $A$ and $B$?
column2: $|A| = |B|$ iff there exists a bijection $f: A \to B$ — a one-to-one correspondence, with no reliance on counting or arithmetic.

column1: State the Dedekind definition of an infinite set and give the classic example.
column2: A set is infinite (Dedekind-infinite) if it is in bijection with one of its own proper subsets. Example: $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$, $f(n) = n+1$, is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto its proper subset of positive integers.

column1: What is $\aleph_0$ and what condition characterizes a countable set?
column2: $\aleph_0$ (aleph-null) is the cardinality of $\mathbb{N}$, the smallest infinite cardinality. A set $S$ is countable iff there exists an injection $f: S \to \mathbb{N}$, equivalent to being able to list its elements as a sequence $s_0, s_1, s_2, \ldots$
